body.text: Wilfred Luiramo walks to the coast every morning to check the seaweed stakes in the shallows. He wades in, clearing the overnight debris, checking each line with his hands, slowly and methodically. But he has to wait: it has rained non-stop for the past few days.

Luiramo owns Haleta Seaweed, a local enterprise in Solomon Islands’ Western Province that provides employment for many families. “The weather pattern keeps changing and it’s impossible to predict,” he said. “Today it will rain, tomorrow it’s sunny, and it keeps changing all the time.”
El Niño has brought strong winds and continuous rain. Seaweed farming is highly sensitive to these shifts: growth depends on suitable temperatures, salinity, currents, and tides.

“Sometimes, we do not have sunlight for the whole week,” Luiramo said. “When there is constant rainfall, the seaweed cannot dry because we use sunlight to dry the products. When the seaweed products are slow to dry, we cannot package and sell them. This affects the income of everyone in the community.”

Weather variability is not the only pressure Luiramo’s community has faced. In April, Tropical Cyclone Maila destroyed every seaweed farm in the community, he said. More recently, the low-tide period has extended well beyond its usual window.
“The normal low tide period is around June,” Luiramo said. “But for this year, we still experience low tide from June, July, and August.”
“El Niño is already here,” he said, “and we need to quickly adapt.”
El Niño disrupts patterns

On a map, the Pacific Islands are specks that can be passed over unnoticed. Palau lies east of the Philippines and north of Australia. Solomon Islands lie further south-east along a curve that ends with Fiji. They sit like pebbles in the vastness of the Pacific Ocean, and the ocean is changing.

The 2026-27 El Niño is strengthening into what forecasters warn could be a “super” event. China’s National Climate Centre has said it is developing rapidly and could become the strongest since instrumental records began. Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific were more than 2.5°C above normal in the first half of August.

For farmers whose livelihoods depend on the sea and the weather, this is not a distant climate projection. Their work rests on close knowledge of local conditions—the tides, rainfall, temperatures, and seasonal change. That knowledge guides when to plant and when to harvest, when to act and when to wait. As those patterns become less predictable, farming gets harder, with El Niño compounding the effects of longer-term climate change.
Livelihoods at stake

Aquaculture is a source of income for many island communities. Across the Pacific Islands, it generates an estimated US$130-180 million a year, roughly 0.5 per cent of regional GDP. In the Solomon Islands, fisheries and aquaculture account for 7 per cent of national GDP.
At the household level, seaweed farmers in Wagina, a regional hub in Solomon Islands, can earn US$1,200 a month, compared with a national average annual income of US$800.

In Fiji, tilapia-farming households can earn US$1,600 gross and about US$700 net per production cycle. Wild mud crab fishers in Fiji, 88 per cent of whom are Indigenous women, can earn 60-70 Fijian dollars a week from selling crabs, fish, and other marine resources, income that pays for school fees and daily needs.
Farming under strain
In Fiji, Katarina Senabu Baleisuva watches her tilapia ponds, checking the water quality. She feeds the fish three times a day.

Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia was introduced to Fiji in 1998 to support long-term food security and rural livelihoods. Today, Fiji is the largest producer of tilapia in the Pacific, at about 400 tonnes a year. More than 350 tilapia farms operate across the country, mostly at subsistence and semi-commercial levels.
Baleisuva won the Tilapia Farmer of the Year award at Fiji’s National Women in Agriculture Awards. She describes her work as getting harder.
“When it’s very hot, the water level goes down,” she said. “And when the rains come, the water turns very cold and sometimes the ponds flood.”
“It really affects our production,” she said. “We’re finding it hard to make a livelihood.”

She is trying to adapt. “I cannot rely on aquaculture alone. I have to do both agriculture and aquaculture.” She has dug more ponds to store water for dry spells, with some government support. “I’m finding it difficult to find financial support, for my aquaculture especially,” she said.
Also in Fiji, the mud crab farmer Tarusila Veibi uses bamboo and tree bark to make cages for mud crab farming. She visits the cages two or three times a day to feed the crabs.

“At this time of the year, we start to have rain,” Veibi said. “But now it’s really dry and cold and windy. The trees are starting to die. We try to plant but the dry soil is very hard to dig. There is no green grass for cows, and the river water level is slowly going down.”
In Palau, the giant clam farmer Patty Kloulechad is also adapting to unusually hot, dry weather that has left soil parched, grass browning, and tap water running warm.
Giant clam aquaculture has been a source of livelihood and a tool for reef restoration in the Pacific for decades.

But high coastal water temperatures and low rainfall have accelerated algal growth in her clam cages, smothering the clams. Deep-water cage placement, once a strategy to protect the clams, now makes routine cleaning harder.
“We have adjusted our maintenance schedule to align with the lowest tides to allow sufficient time to thoroughly clean the cages,” Kloulechad said.
Besides clam farming, her community is switching to weather-resilient crops at the main farm and moving vulnerable crops closer to home for better care.
Adapting without certainty
Across the Pacific, aquaculture farmers are learning and adjusting to a world where the weather no longer follows old patterns.
Luiramo has changed his routine completely, seizing every fleeting spell of favourable weather. “When there is sunlight, we have to be there. We cannot waste any time.”
The constraint is hard: it keeps farmers from moving around and doing other family errands. “We cannot move freely, we need to stay by the coast nearly every day, waiting,” he said.

Luiramo also wants seaweed farmers to diversify into short-term crops such as cabbage, aubergine, and tomatoes to meet basic needs. “For those of us on the islands, we don’t have many options, but we need to build resilience,” he said.
Water conservation is a priority across their operations.

Baleisuva has dug boreholes to reach groundwater during water shortages, and tilapia farmers near creeks are filling standby ponds to top up production ponds during droughts. Some are also growing vegetables alongside their fish, reusing pond water. Island communities rely heavily on water tanks for drinking and for work such as washing seaweed and fish cages, so stored water must serve both households and farms.
Veibi is rotating her cattle to wherever green pasture can be found and planting crops in swampy areas that have not yet dried out.

The farmers are clear that they cannot adapt alone. “We really need to work together with the government,” Baleisuva said, adding that many rural farmers are left behind and their voices are not heard.

Luiramo said solidarity has kept seaweed farming alive in his community for around 40 years, even without consistent commercial or government support. He also stressed the need for policy reform: “The existing gaps between government and communities delay responses to farmers’ needs. We need policies that can integrate local knowledge, seaweed farming expertise, and scientific research.”
But El Niño cannot be farmed around. It is a shock to the entire system, and what is lost in this shift is certainty.

Long-held knowledge of when to plant or harvest, when to dry or when to wait is becoming harder to rely on. Luiramo used to know that three or four days of sun would dry his seaweed. Now he cannot be sure from one morning to the next what the weather will bring. Baleisuva once knew when the rains would come, but now the rain arrives without warning, followed by heat that dries up her fishponds. Veibi knew which months would bring green pastures for her cattle. But she now faces a dry, cold, windy spell that is lowering the rivers. Kloulechad knew the tides well enough to plan her work. Now the water runs warm, algae blooms, and she earns less than she used to.
Advice from the frontlines
Asked what advice they would give other farmers, especially those in South and South-East Asia who are about to face El Niño’s effects, the four share one message: prepare early and adapt.

Luiramo’s message is to be alert: “We are now living in changing times and what really needs to be done is we keep monitoring our products. We keep monitoring the changing weather patterns and when there is a favourable weather, we have to do something to maintain our livelihoods.”
Baleisuva’s advice is practical: “Try to work smart. Don’t rely on one commodity but do integrated farming.”
Veibi offers calm preparedness: “Don’t start to panic, whatever comes let it come. But get prepared before it gets worse.”

Kloulechad, drawing on her community’s past experience, advises: “We have been in El Niño conditions before. We try to review past strategies, adapt successful practices to our current situation, and conserve our existing resources.”
Melissa Gonzalez is Research Associate, SEI.
